title: Preface
summary: Exxon Mobil Corporation’s 2022 Form 10-K annual report covers the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022. It identifies the company, its New Jersey incorporation, Texas headquarters, contact number, SEC file number, and NYSE-listed common stock and notes. The filing reports issuer status and compliance checkboxes, including large accelerated filer and internal-control attestation; market value of nonaffiliate voting stock exceeded $356 billion, with 4,070,984,988 common shares outstanding as of January 31, 2023. The 2023 proxy statement is incorporated by reference for Part III.

title: EXXON MOBIL CORPORATION FORM 10-K FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED DECEMBER 31, 2022
summary: The text is the table of contents for Exxon Mobil Corporation’s 2022 Form 10-K. It lists Parts I–IV, covering business, risks, properties, legal matters, market and operating results, financial statements, controls, governance, compensation, ownership, related-party matters, accounting fees, exhibits, and the Form 10-K summary. It also identifies the financial section, exhibit index, signatures, certifications, and page references.

title: PART I

nodes.title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s history, global operations, core oil, gas, petrochemical, specialty-product, and lower-emission businesses, research, affiliates, and competitive environment are outlined, with references to segment and reserves data elsewhere in the report. The text describes patents and licensing, long-term employee development, workforce diversity and headcount, environmental compliance and spending (including projected increases), and where to find information on regulatory, supply, seasonality, contract, and foreign-operation risks. It also explains the company website’s SEC filings and governance materials and the SEC’s public information site.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Supply and Demand
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil faces risks from commodity price and margin volatility, which can harm different segments differently, and from uncertain markets, policies, and technology for lower-emission businesses. Results may be affected by economic conditions, recessions, geopolitical, regulatory, trade, health, financial-market, currency, and pandemic-related developments; changing demand from efficiency, weather, alternatives, technology, preferences, and incomes; supply changes from new sources, capacity, quotas, emissions policies, conflict, disasters, operational or logistics disruptions, and technology; and interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, and potential losses on hedging or trading instruments.

nodes.title: Government and Political Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s performance may be harmed by political and regulatory developments, including limits on resource access, investment, trade, and permitted business; sanctions that disadvantage the company; and weak or uncertain legal systems that enable unpredictable government action and impede contract enforcement. Risks in all jurisdictions include tax and royalty increases, price controls, changing environmental and other regulations, delayed permits or restricted transport, mandated standards, disclosure rules, contract changes, currency actions, and expropriation. Litigation, enforcement, punitive damages, and policy-driven lawsuits may also cause losses, while unrest, sabotage, terrorism, cyberattacks, and national-security restrictions can raise security costs or interrupt operations.

nodes.title: Climate Change and the Energy Transition
nodes.summary: The text discusses ExxonMobil’s climate-transition risks and strategy: uncertain net-zero scenarios and the need to identify energy-system changes and time investments appropriately; government and indirect measures to cut emissions that may raise costs, weaken hydrocarbon demand or competitiveness, delay projects, and increase compliance burdens; development of lower-emission technologies—including CCS, hydrogen, and fuels—through research and partnerships, with business success dependent on cost-competitive deployment; and reliance on supportive policies and markets. Delays, policy reversals, or restricting hydrocarbon supply without matching demand reductions could cause volatility, inflation, energy shortages, and harm businesses.

nodes.title: Operational and Other Factors
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s results depend on managing controllable operational risks and, for non-operated projects, the performance of co-venturers. Key factors include successful exploration and development; effective project and portfolio management, including partnerships, cost and schedule control, markets, technical risks, diversification, and asset divestments and liabilities; operational efficiency and employee capabilities; research, development, and adoption of technology, including emissions-reduction and data-processing advances; safety, environmental, enterprise-risk, and internal-control systems; cybersecurity defenses and third-party exposure; preparedness for severe weather and other disruptions; limited insurance availability and affordability; competition from private and state-owned firms, service companies, and alternative energy; and reputational risks. These factors may affect returns, operations, financing, approvals, talent, demand, and forward-looking plans and results.

ExxonMobil faces risks from volatile commodity prices, margins, demand, supply, economic and financial conditions, and uncertain markets for lower-emission businesses. Political, legal, and regulatory actions—including taxes, sanctions, permits, environmental rules, litigation, unrest, and security restrictions—may disrupt operations or raise costs. Climate-transition risks include uncertain pathways, policies, technology, markets, and investment timing. Operational risks span exploration, projects, partners, costs, technology, safety, controls, cybersecurity, disruptions, insurance, competition, and reputation, affecting returns, approvals, talent, demand, and plans.

It describes technologies and geological, engineering, production, seismic, and analog data used for 2022 additions, plus the expertise, oversight duties, database controls, review approvals, and audit procedures of the Global Reserves and Resources group.

nodes.title: 2. Proved Undeveloped Reserves
nodes.summary: At year-end 2022, ExxonMobil reported 6.6 GOEB of proved undeveloped reserves (37% of total proved reserves), up from 6.3 GOEB in 2021. Development transferred 1.0 GOEB to developed reserves; extensions and discoveries added 1.4 GOEB, Asian purchases added 0.7 GOEB, and 0.8 GOEB were reclassified as no longer proved. The company invested $12.1 billion to advance these reserves, 71% of Upstream capital and exploration spending. It explains long development timelines, infrastructure constraints, factors affecting recovery, and country-specific projects in Australia, Kazakhstan, and the UAE; over 80% of reserves undeveloped for at least five years are in those countries and the United States. The text also presents 2020–2022 oil, gas, liquids, and oil-equivalent production by product, geography, and consolidated subsidiaries versus equity companies, with an Other Americas footnote.

summary: Reports ExxonMobil’s year-end 2022 proved reserves by product, geography, development status, and ownership, describing estimation methods, data and technologies, uncertainty and risks, funding requirements, and the Global Reserves and Resources group’s expertise, controls, reviews, and audits. Details proved undeveloped reserves, their year-over-year changes, development spending, delays and constraints, and key projects and countries, and presents 2020–2022 production by product, geography, and ownership.

Describes Syncrude and Kearl oil-sands mining operations, ownership interests, acreage, extraction and processing methods, product handling, location, and 2022 net production.

title: A. Wells Drilling

nodes.title: Equity Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports year-end 2022 and 2021 gross and net wells drilling by region and subsidiary type: consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies, across the United States, Canada/Other Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia/Oceania. Total wells were 910 gross/525 net in 2022 versus 1,141 gross/628 net in 2021. It also reviews U.S. activities: ExxonMobil held 9.5 million net acres at year-end 2022, including 0.2 million offshore, and relinquished 1 million acres, including 0.2 million offshore. Operations spanned the lower 48 states and Alaska; Golden Pass LNG development continued, and 519.9 net exploratory and development wells were completed in the inland lower 48, focused mainly on liquids-rich Permian Basin opportunities. Gulf of Mexico holdings were 0.1 million net acres, with 0.9 net development wells completed; Alaska production and development continued, with 2.6 net development wells completed.

nodes.title: Canada / Other Americas
key_items: Oil and Gas Operations; In Situ Bitumen Operations
nodes.summary: In 2022, ExxonMobil reported acreage, well completions, and project activity across Canada and other Americas. Canada held 4.3 million net oil and gas acres, relinquished 2.5 million, and completed 1.3 net exploratory and development wells; its in situ operations held 0.5 million acres and completed 24 Cold Lake development wells. Argentina held 2.9 million acres and completed 5.4 development wells. Brazil held 2.6 million offshore acres, completed 1.5 exploratory wells, and continued Bacalhau Phase 1 development. Guyana held 4.6 million offshore acres, completed six wells, began Liza Phase 2 Unity operations, continued Payara development, and funded Yellowtail.

nodes.title: Europe
nodes.summary: At year-end 2022, ExxonMobil held 1.4 million net onshore acres in Germany; 1.4 million net licensed acres in the Netherlands (0.4 million offshore), where it completed 0.2 net development well as the Dutch Government further reduced Groningen gas extraction and considered when to end production; and 0.1 million offshore licensed acres in the United Kingdom. In Africa, it held 3 million acres in Angola (2.9 million offshore), completing 3.3 net exploratory and development wells; 0.1 million offshore acres in Equatorial Guinea; and 0.7 million offshore acres in Mozambique, after relinquishing 1 million acres outside Area 4, while Coral South Floating LNG began production in October. Nigeria acreage was 0.9 million offshore acres, with 0.4 net exploratory and development wells completed.

nodes.title: Asia
nodes.summary: The text reports ExxonMobil’s 2022 acreage, development wells, projects, and infrastructure across Asia and Australia/Oceania. It covers activity in Azerbaijan, Indonesia, Iraq, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Qatar, Russia, Thailand, the UAE, Australia, and Papua New Guinea, including acreage relinquishments, project progress, LNG and gas capacity, and Russia’s terminated Sakhalin interests. Worldwide exploration held 18.8 million net acres and completed 1.2 net exploratory wells. Delivery commitments for 2023–2025 total about 36 million barrels of oil and 2.3 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, to be met mainly from proved developed reserves, with other reserves or market purchases as needed.

nodes.title: 2022 Regional Acreage and Development
nodes.summary: The page reports ExxonMobil’s 2022 acreage, well activity, and development projects in the UAE, Australia, and Papua New Guinea. UAE activity included 81,000 net offshore acres, 2.8 net development wells, and continued Upper Zakum sustainment work. Australia had 1.2 million offshore and 10,000 onshore acres, relinquished 600,000 offshore acres, and continued Gorgon Stage 2 and Jansz Io Compression; it also describes Gorgon Jansz LNG and domestic gas facilities. Papua New Guinea had 2.1 million onshore acres, relinquished 1.2 million offshore acres, and its integrated LNG development is outlined. Worldwide exploration outside established production areas held 18.8 million net acres and completed 1.2 net exploratory wells.

summary: Reports 2021–2022 gross and net wells drilled by region and subsidiary type, then summarizes ExxonMobil’s 2022 acreage, relinquishments, well completions, exploration, and development across the United States, Canada and other Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia, and Papua New Guinea. It covers regional projects and infrastructure, LNG and gas developments, Russia’s terminated Sakhalin interests, worldwide exploration acreage and wells, and 2023–2025 oil and gas delivery commitments and their expected sources.

title: 6. Delivery Commitments
summary: ExxonMobil has crude oil and natural gas sales obligations, including some fixed-quantity contracts extending beyond one year; gas contracts may be supplied by its production or the spot market. For 2023–2025, it is committed to deliver about 36 million barrels of oil and 2.3 trillion cubic feet of gas, mainly from proved developed reserves, with remaining volumes supplied from proved undeveloped reserves or open-market purchases as needed.

title: 7. Oil and Gas Properties, Wells, Operations and Acreage
summary: Reports year-end 2022 and 2021 gross and net productive oil and gas wells by region for consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies, plus total counts. It also gives operated-well counts and wells with multiple completions for both years. Developed acreage (gross and net, in thousands of acres) is reported by region and entity type for both years; notes specify Other Americas acreage figures, a restatement of 2021 European acreage, and that oil and gas acreage is not tracked separately because both may be produced from the same acreage.

title: C. Gross and Net Undeveloped Acreage

nodes.title: Consolidated Subsidiaries
nodes.summary: The text reports ExxonMobil’s gross and net undeveloped acreage by region for consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies at year-end 2022 and 2021, including total acreage and notes on Other Americas figures and a restatement of 2021 Europe data. It explains that acreage rights depend on property-specific contracts; work programs assess exploration potential before expiration, acreage may be relinquished or extensions sought, and scheduled expirations over the next three years are not expected to materially harm the Corporation.

nodes.title: Equity Companies
nodes.summary: The text reports ExxonMobil’s gross and net developed acreage for 2022 and 2021 by region and ownership type (consolidated subsidiaries and equity companies), and undeveloped acreage for the same years, with notes on Other Americas and restated European figures. Oil and gas acreage is not reported separately because both may be produced from the same land. Acreage consists of concessions, blocks, and leases with property-specific rights; work programs evaluate exploration potential, acreage may be relinquished or extensions obtained, and expirations over the next three years are not expected to materially harm the company. In the United States, exploration and production rights are generally leased from government or private mineral owners, with exploration terms typically lasting one to ten years and production terms usually continuing until production ceases; some leases can continue beyond exploration, and fee interests may be acquired.

nodes.title: Canada / Other Americas
nodes.summary: The text outlines hydrocarbon license and contract terms in Canada, Argentina, Brazil, and Guyana. Canada’s onshore rights vary in duration and may be renewed or extended, generally continuing while production is proven; offshore exploration licenses last nine years and require work commitments and rentals, production licenses last 25 years with possible extensions, and significant discovery licenses have no fixed term. Argentina’s 2014 law sets 35-year unconventional and 25-year conventional onshore concessions, with unlimited 10-year extensions after development; offshore licenses granted in 2019 last eight years in two four-year phases, with an optional five-year extension per license. Brazil’s concession contracts allow up to eight years for exploration and 27 for production, while production-sharing contracts allow up to seven and 28 years, respectively. Guyana may grant licenses and petroleum agreements, which provide up to 10 years for exploration and 20 years for production, extendable by 10 years.

nodes.title: Europe
nodes.summary: European licensing terms vary by country. Germany grants exploration concessions for up to five years, extendable repeatedly by up to three years subject to work commitments; production licenses typically last 20–25 years and may be extended while production continues. In the Netherlands, licenses issued since 2003 have terms specified according to required activities, while earlier production rights retain their original conditions: onshore licenses were indefinite before 1988 or lasted 35–45 years thereafter; offshore licenses lasted 40 years before 1976 or 15–40 years thereafter. UK terms are government-set: older licenses commonly had six-year initial terms, acreage relinquishment, and possible 40-year extensions with different outcomes for producing, developing, and other areas. Most current traditional licenses have four-year exploration and extension terms, followed by 18 years for production, with required acreage relinquishments.

nodes.title: Africa
nodes.summary: The text outlines oil and gas contract frameworks, exploration and production periods, extensions, and key changes across African and Asian countries. It covers Angola, Equatorial Guinea, Mozambique, Nigeria, Azerbaijan, Indonesia, Iraq, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Qatar, Russia, Thailand, and the UAE. Notable details include Mozambique acreage relinquishments, Nigeria’s 2021 Petroleum Industry Act and lease transitions, Azerbaijan’s PSA extension to 2049, Russia’s 2022 termination and transfer of Sakhalin interests, and the UAE’s Upper Zakum agreements extended to 2051.

nodes.title: Australia / Oceania
nodes.summary: Australia’s offshore Commonwealth petroleum activities are federally regulated: exploration permits last six years, with two possible five-year renewals; retention leases cover resources expected to become viable within 15 years and run for renewable five-year periods. Production licenses issued before July 1998 lasted 21 years, renewable for another 21 and then indefinitely; newer licenses are indefinite, but either may end after five years without production. Papua New Guinea’s Oil and Gas Act provides prospecting licenses for six years, usually with a five-year extension and possible three-year additional extension, with 50% area relinquishment generally required; development licenses last 25 years, with discretionary extensions of up to 20 years. Retention licenses for gas expected to become viable within 15 years run five years and may be extended twice at ministerial discretion, up to that maximum.

nodes.summary: ExxonMobil manufactures, trades, and sells petroleum products through a global network of plants, transportation systems, and distribution centers supplying fuels, lubricants, feedstocks, and other products. The page lists year-end 2022 refining capacity locations and regional totals for the United States, Canada, Europe, and Asia Pacific.

nodes.title: Middle East
nodes.summary: The text lists refinery locations by region and country, product categories, ExxonMobil’s share of capacity in thousands of barrels per day, and ownership interests. It explains capacity calculation and reporting conventions, notes the exclusion of a minor Qatar interest, and flags assets with announced sales expected to close in 2023. It also introduces year-end 2022 retail fuel-site counts by ownership type and region, noting sales through Exxon, Esso, and Mobil brands.

nodes.title: Worldwide
nodes.summary: A worldwide table presents several numerical figures. Notes state that the Corporation agreed in October 2022 to sell the Billings refinery and select midstream assets, including about 300 retail fuel sites, to Par Pacific Holdings; in December 2022, it agreed to sell its Italy fuels business, including about 2,300 sites, to Italiana Petroli; and in January 2023, it announced the sale of its interest in Esso Thailand, with about 800 sites. Each transaction was expected to close in 2023.

nodes.title: Chemical Complex Capacity by Region
key_items: Information with regard to chemical complex capacity:
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil manufactures and sells petrochemicals, with integrated complexes supplying olefins, polyolefins and other products. The page reports year-end 2022 ethylene, polyethylene and polypropylene capacity, ExxonMobil interests and regional and worldwide totals across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia Pacific. Capacity accounting reflects full output at majority-owned subsidiaries and ExxonMobil’s share at companies it owns 50% or less; figures may not sum exactly due to rounding.

nodes.title: ITEM 3. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil uses a $1 million threshold for disclosing environmental proceedings. XTO received DOJ notice in August 2022 of a potential EPA civil action alleging Clean Air Act General Duty Clause violations linked to the 2018 Schnegg well blowout in Ohio; no action or draft decree has been filed, penalties were unquantified, and XTO disputes DOJ’s indication that penalties may substantially exceed $1 million. In November 2022, Texas sued ExxonMobil over alleged 2018–2022 air-emissions violations at the Baytown Olefins Plant, seeking penalties above $1 million, injunctive relief, and litigation costs. Further details are in Note 16.

nodes.title: ITEM 4. MINE SAFETY DISCLOSURES
nodes.summary: Item 4 states that mine safety disclosures are not applicable. The document lists ExxonMobil executive officers, their ages as of February 22, 2023, current roles, and selected positions held during the prior five years. It also notes that officers are generally elected by the Board at its annual election meeting and serve until successors are elected and qualified; the listed officers must file reports under Section 16 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

nodes.title: BUSINESS PROFILE
nodes.summary: Business profile tables compare 2022 and 2021 financial and operating results by segment and U.S./non-U.S./total: earnings after tax, average capital employed, return on average capital employed, and capital and exploration expenditures, plus production, refinery throughput, and Energy, Chemical, and Specialty Products sales. Notes define the capital measures, explain natural-gas conversion to oil-equivalent barrels and sales reported net of same-counterparty contracts, and caution that rounding may affect totals.

nodes.title: FINANCIAL INFORMATION
FINANCIAL INFORMATION (intro)
nodes.summary: The text presents ExxonMobil’s 2020–2022 financial information, including revenue, earnings, returns, working capital, investment, assets, debt, equity, share counts, and employee numbers, with notes defining net debt and regular employees. It then defines the non-GAAP cash flow from operations and asset sales measure and reports its components and totals for each year. Finally, it defines capital employed from both business asset-and-liability and corporate debt-and-equity perspectives and provides the calculations and totals for 2020–2022.

nodes.title: Cash Flow From Operations and Asset Sales
nodes.summary: Defines ExxonMobil’s non-GAAP cash flow from operations and asset sales as operating cash flow plus proceeds from asset sales and investment sales or returns, explaining its usefulness in assessing funds available for investment and financing. Reports totals for 2022–2020: $82.044 billion, $51.305 billion, and $15.667 billion. Defines capital employed as net investment, presented from business asset/liability and corporate debt/equity perspectives, including equity-company shares; provides reconciliation figures for 2022–2020, with totals of $238.166 billion, $218.642 billion, and $227.137 billion.

nodes.title: Capital Employed
nodes.summary: Defines ExxonMobil’s non-GAAP measures and provides 2020–2022 figures. Cash flow from operations and asset sales combines operating cash flow with proceeds and returns from asset divestitures, explaining its use in assessing funds available for investment and financing. Capital employed is presented from both business asset/liability and corporate debt/equity perspectives, including equity-company interests. Return on average capital employed (ROCE) is defined for segments and the corporation, with financing costs excluded; its historical productivity role and complementary use of cash-flow measures for investment decisions are noted.

nodes.title: Return on Average Capital Employed
nodes.summary: Defines non-GAAP return on average capital employed (ROCE): segment earnings, including equity-company earnings and excluding financing costs, divided by average segment capital; corporate ROCE uses ExxonMobil-attributable net income less after-tax financing costs over average corporate capital. The company says it consistently applies ROCE as a measure of historical capital productivity, while using more cash-flow-based measures for investment decisions. A 2020–2022 table reports net income, financing-cost components, earnings excluding financing costs, average capital employed, and corporate ROCE: 24.9% (2022), 10.9% (2021), and (9.3)% (2020).

nodes.title: Structural Cost Savings
nodes.summary: Defines structural cost savings as sustainable expense reductions from efficiencies, workforce reductions, and other measures relative to 2019; estimated cumulative annual savings totaled $7 billion. Changes in expenses also reflect market factors, activity levels, and new operations, and estimates may be revised based on sustainability. Management uses the internally stewarded measure to oversee spending, and it helps investors understand disciplined expense optimization. A calculation section is labeled in billions of dollars.

nodes.title: Components of operating costs From ExxonMobil’s Consolidated Statement of Income (U.S. GAAP)
nodes.summary: The text presents ExxonMobil operating-cost components and reconciliations for 2019 and 2022, including total operating costs, cash operating expenses, energy and production taxes, and a cash-opex bridge. It defines non-GAAP earnings excluding significant identified items and explains their purpose and limitations. It then provides 2020–2022 U.S., non-U.S., and total segment earnings reconciliations for Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, and Specialty Products, listing adjustments such as impairments, asset-sale gains or losses, inventory valuation, tax-related items, contractual provisions, and other identified items.

nodes.title: Frequently Used Terms and Segment Earnings
nodes.summary: Defines non-GAAP earnings excluding Identified Items as earnings adjusted for significant non-operational events, generally with a corporate quarterly impact of at least $250 million; segment impacts may be smaller when events span segments or periods. Explains management’s use of the measure for comparability and transparency, and that it does not replace U.S. GAAP net income. Lists earnings reconciliation categories for Upstream, Energy Products, and Chemical Products, including impairments, tax-related items, and other identified items; Upstream also includes asset-sale gains or losses, inventory valuation, and contractual provisions.

nodes.title: Specialty Products
nodes.summary: The text presents Specialty Products earnings (loss) by U.S., non-U.S., and total for 2020–2022, reconciling U.S. GAAP results to non-GAAP results excluding identified items such as impairments, asset-sale gains or losses, tax-related items, and other adjustments. It also reports Corporate and Financing results and identified-item adjustments for 2020–2022, plus Corporate total net income attributable to ExxonMobil and its reconciliation to non-GAAP earnings. Notes define Corporate earnings by reference to the consolidated income statement, clarify that segment results and earnings per share exclude noncontrolling interests unless stated otherwise, and warn that rounding may cause totals not to add precisely.

nodes.title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS
nodes.summary: The section defines forward-looking statements, including financial, operational, strategic, emissions, low-carbon technology, project, production, and shareholder-return plans, and warns that actual outcomes may differ materially. It lists market, economic, policy, geopolitical, regulatory, operational, technological, and other risks, referring readers to Item 1A. Sustainability statements may use evolving standards and assumptions and are not necessarily material to investors. Energy scenarios are uncertain, not predictions or endorsements; third-party scenarios are their authors’ work, and ExxonMobil invests through its own planning process. “Project” may have varied meanings.

nodes.title: OVERVIEW
nodes.summary: Management says its financial reporting reflects ExxonMobil’s integrated operations across oil and gas, products, specialty products, and lower-emission opportunities. Its segments are Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, and Specialty Products; since April 2022, Chemical and Downstream have been combined in Product Solutions, alongside Upstream and developing Low Carbon Solutions, supported by shared technology and services. The integrated model and resources help manage commodity-price risk and enable investment in energy supplies. Annual Corporate Plans, grounded in the Outlook for Energy and field production profiles, set objectives and investment assumptions for prices, margins, volumes, costs, emissions pricing, and exchange rates. Projects are assessed under varied market conditions and reappraised to capture lessons.

nodes.title: BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT
Long-Term Business Outlook
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil’s Outlook projects energy supply and demand through 2050 to guide planning, while acknowledging uncertainty and using scenarios, including stringent climate pathways, to track transition signposts. It forecasts population and economic growth, rising global energy demand led by non-OECD countries, efficiency gains, and changing electricity, transport, industry, and building needs. Oil and gas remain important, with growing renewables, nuclear, and natural gas; meeting demand requires substantial, timely investment. The text describes lower-carbon technologies—electrification, hydrogen, lower-emission fuels, and carbon capture—and evolving climate policies, including assumed regional carbon costs and Paris Agreement commitments. Projections draw on company analysis and external sources.

nodes.title: Progress Reducing Emissions
nodes.summary: The Corporation aims to use its scale, integration, technology, and people to grow earnings and cash flow while supporting the energy transition and preserving investment flexibility. With technological progress and consistent policy support, it targets net-zero operated Scope 1 and 2 emissions by 2050, including net-zero Permian operated assets by 2030; asset roadmaps were completed in 2022 and may be updated as conditions evolve, since some measures are currently unaffordable. Relative to 2016, 2030 goals include reductions in corporate-wide and upstream emissions intensity, methane intensity, and flaring intensity, alongside absolute cuts in emissions and flaring and achieving World Bank Zero Routine Flaring. These plans cover operated assets’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions. Since 2021, Low Carbon Solutions has expanded opportunities in carbon capture and storage, hydrogen, and lower-emission fuels, using company capabilities to cut its own and customers’ emissions. Investments will develop and scale these technologies, whose deployment depends on policy support and technological advances.

nodes.title: Recent Business Environment
nodes.summary: The text describes pre- and pandemic-era underinvestment, refining capacity closures, supply constraints, and recovering demand that lifted oil, gas, and refining prices and margins in 2021–22; chemical margins later fell amid weak demand and capacity additions. Prices remain volatile amid economic and geopolitical uncertainty. It outlines inflation’s causes and persistence, and the Corporation’s efforts to manage cost impacts. Organizational changes delivered $7 billion in structural savings versus 2019, including about $2 billion annually from workforce reductions, while ongoing streamlining aims to improve effectiveness, market focus, and resource allocation.

nodes.title: Russia-Ukraine Conflict
nodes.summary: In 2022, the Corporation announced it would exit Russia’s Sakhalin-1 project after the invasion of Ukraine, recording a $3.4 billion after-tax impairment. Despite good-faith exit efforts amid sanctions, Russian decrees effective October 14 transferred its interests to a Russian operator; the fourth quarter included a $1.1 billion after-tax benefit related largely to changed obligations. The exit removed about 150 million oil-equivalent barrels from proved reserves. The Corporation also holds interests in Kazakhstan oil fields and the CPC export pipeline, whose Russian route could be disrupted by countermeasures to sanctions, potentially causing uncertain-duration cash-flow losses. Kazakhstan interests generated about $2.5 billion in 2022 after-tax earnings and 246,000 barrels of oil-equivalent daily production.

nodes.title: Additional European Taxes on the Energy Sector
nodes.summary: The EU’s 2022 emergency energy-price regulation required at least a 33% tax on qualifying oil, coal, gas, and refining companies’ 2022 and/or 2023 profits above 120% of their 2018–2021 average, implemented by the end of 2022. EU and UK measures caused ExxonMobil an approximately $1.8 billion after-tax charge in fourth-quarter 2022; future earnings reductions could reach $2 billion, depending on commodity prices and taxable income. ExxonMobil’s Upstream strategy prioritizes selective, low-cost, value-adding development, technology, efficiency, emissions reduction, operational excellence, employees, and communities. Production is expected to shift toward the Americas and unconventional, deepwater, and LNG resources. Projects in Guyana, Brazil, the Permian, and LNG markets could add capacity, though volumes depend on project timing, operations, reservoirs, regulation, commercial terms, asset sales, weather, prices, investment, and trade conditions. Long-term prices reflect demand drivers such as economic activity, prosperity, technology, preferences, and policy, and supply factors including politics, OPEC and other resource owners, and alternative energy.

nodes.title: Key Recent Events
nodes.summary: The text highlights 2022 developments: Guyana’s 10 Stabroek discoveries, Liza Phase 2 start-up and strong production, accelerated Payara timing, and Yellowtail’s expected 2025 first oil; progress on Brazil’s Bacalhau project; Permian production growth, improved drilling and capital efficiency, and emissions-reduction initiatives toward 2030 net-zero Scope 1 and 2 emissions; and LNG portfolio expansion through Qatar North Field East, Coral South production, Papua New Guinea milestones, and Golden Pass’s planned 2024 start-up. It also presents Upstream U.S. and non-U.S. GAAP earnings, identified items, and earnings excluding identified items for 2022, 2021, and 2020, with a reference to definitions.

nodes.title: 2022 Upstream Earnings Factor Analysis
nodes.summary: The text analyzes 2022 and 2021 Upstream earnings factors: higher realizations drove large gains, while volume/mix and other costs had mixed effects; identified losses reflected impairments, contractual provisions, Russia’s expropriation, European taxes, and asset-sale gains. It reports 2020–2022 regional crude/NGL/bitumen/synthetic oil, natural gas, and oil-equivalent production, noting the conversion ratio, and introduces a 2022-versus-2021 oil-equivalent volume reconciliation by entitlements, government mandates, divestments, and growth/other.

nodes.title: Current Year
nodes.summary: The text reports current production-volume figures and explains that natural gas is converted to oil-equivalent units at six million cubic feet per thousand barrels. Production rose 25 thousand barrels per day in 2022 versus 2021 to 3.7 million, as Permian and Guyana growth and easing government curtailments outweighed divestments, Russia expropriation, and lower price-related entitlements. In 2021, production fell 49 thousand barrels per day versus 2020 because lower entitlements, decline, and divestments outweighed demand and growth. It defines reconciliation factors: permanent net-interest entitlement changes; temporary price, spending, and other entitlement changes; government production limits or sanctions; divestments; and all remaining operational or non-operational influences, including projects, acquisitions, downtime, demand, natural decline, and fiscal or commercial terms.

nodes.title: Energy Products
key_items: Energy Products Operational Results; Refinery throughput
nodes.summary: Describes Energy Products’ integrated fuels business, its dependence on refining margins and operational performance, the sharp 2022 margin recovery, and factors driving near-term volatility. Lists Beaumont expansion, Strathcona renewable diesel progress, and planned Billings, Italy Fuels, and Esso Thailand divestitures. Reports 2020–2022 U.S. and non-U.S. earnings, identified items and adjusted earnings; explains 2022 and 2021 earnings drivers; and presents refinery throughput and product sales by region and category.

nodes.title: Chemical Products
nodes.summary: Chemical Products is ExxonMobil’s global petrochemical business, supported by scale, integration, proprietary technology, operational excellence, investment, and cost discipline. Long-term demand is expected to outpace economic growth. In 2022, industry margins fell below their historical range, but earnings stayed above the segment’s 10-year average. Recent developments include a 450,000-tonne-per-year polypropylene expansion in Baton Rouge, an advanced recycling facility in Baytown processing over 80 million pounds of plastic waste annually, and ongoing chemical projects in Baytown and Huizhou, China. Earnings were $3.543 billion in 2022, $6.989 billion in 2021, and $2.257 billion in 2020; 2020 included $105 million in identified impairment losses. In 2022, lower margins, product mix, and other costs reduced earnings by $3.030 billion, $170 million, and $250 million, respectively. In 2021, stronger margins, higher volumes, and lower expenses increased earnings by $4.370 billion, $130 million, and $130 million. Worldwide chemical prime product sales were 19.167 million tonnes in 2022, 19.142 million in 2021, and 18.787 million in 2020; regional figures and reporting caveats are also provided.

nodes.title: Specialty Products
key_items: Specialty Products Operational Results; Specialty Products sales (2)
nodes.summary: Specialty Products makes and markets lubricants, basestocks, waxes, synthetics, elastomers, and resins, targeting transportation and industrial efficiency. Lubricant demand is expected to grow; ExxonMobil cites its integration, advantaged projects, and brands. Materia, acquired in 2021, contributes proprietary polymers for infrastructure, oil and gas, and mobility, with scale-up planned. The Singapore Resid Upgrade Project will convert fuel oil into Group II lubricants and clean products. Segment earnings were $2.415 billion in 2022, $3.259 billion in 2021, and $1.201 billion in 2020; excluding identified items, they were $2.455 billion, $2.625 billion, and $1.429 billion, respectively. In 2022, lower margins reduced earnings by $220 million, higher volume added $20 million, and other factors added $30 million; identified items were a $40 million impairment loss versus a $634 million Santoprene-divestment gain in 2021. In 2021, stronger margins, volume, and other factors added $680 million, $300 million, and $220 million; 2020 included $228 million of impairment losses. Worldwide sales were 7.810, 7.666, and 7.237 million metric tons in 2022, 2021, and 2020, respectively.

nodes.title: Corporate and Financing
Corporate and Financing Financial Results
nodes.summary: Corporate and Financing supports operating segments through administration, financing, insurance, and temporarily houses Low Carbon Solutions. Its 2022 loss was $1.663 billion, down from 2021 and 2020, mainly due to lower pension costs, favorable tax impacts, reduced financing costs, and absence of severance costs. Cash rose to $29.7 billion in 2022, driven by strong earnings and depreciation adjustments; uses included capital spending, dividends, share repurchases, debt reduction, and investments. The discussion details 2021–22 operating and investing cash flows, liquidity and credit lines, expected internally generated funding, production-decline risks and project uncertainty, commodity-price sensitivity, investment plans ($22.7 billion in 2022; $23–25 billion planned for 2023), portfolio diversification, asset sales and acquisitions, and monitoring of IBOR reform, which is not considered a material risk.

nodes.title: Asset Management and 2021–2022 Cash Flows
nodes.summary: ExxonMobil reviews asset upgrades, disposals and acquisitions, and considers IBOR reform a nonmaterial risk. Operating cash flow rose to $76.8 billion in 2022 from $48.1 billion in 2021, driven mainly by net income; depreciation, asset-sale adjustments, equity-company dividends and working capital also affected cash. Investing cash use increased to $14.7 billion in 2022 from $10.2 billion in 2021, reflecting higher capital spending and investment activity, partly offset by increased asset-sale and other proceeds.

nodes.title: Financing Cash Flows, Obligations, and Guarantees
nodes.summary: The page compares 2022 and 2021 financing cash flows, dividends, debt reduction, equity changes, and share-repurchase activity. It describes contractual obligations, including leases, debt, retirement and benefit liabilities, purchase commitments, and the $38.2 billion year-end total for take-or-pay and unconditional purchase obligations, with expected 2023–24 payments. It also outlines contingent guarantees and notes they are not expected to materially affect the Corporation’s financial condition or operations.

nodes.title: Financial Strength and Contingencies
nodes.summary: At year-end 2022, the Corporation had $0.3 billion in unused short-term and $1.2 billion in unused long-term committed credit lines. Debt-to-capital and net-debt-to-capital ratios declined from 2020 to 2022. Management considers financial strength strategically important, supporting access to capital markets and major long-term investments. Stronger industry conditions enabled $19.9 billion of debt reduction in 2021 and $6.5 billion in 2022, leaving $41.2 billion in debt. The Corporation says pending lawsuits are not expected to materially affect its operations, financial condition, or financial statements, and reports no other events or uncertainties indicating material future changes; Note 16 provides details.

Corporate and Financing supports operating segments through administration, financing, insurance, and temporary housing of Low Carbon Solutions. The section reviews its 2022 financial results and 2021–22 operating, investing, and financing cash flows; cash, liquidity, credit lines, debt, capital ratios, dividends, share repurchases, and funding plans. It covers capital investment, asset upgrades, sales and acquisitions, diversification, production and commodity-price risks, and IBOR reform. It also details contractual obligations and guarantees, and management’s view that lawsuits and other uncertainties are not expected to materially affect the Corporation.

Covers ExxonMobil’s long-term energy outlook, demand and supply scenarios, climate policy, emissions goals, and investments in lower-carbon technologies; recent market conditions, inflation, restructuring, geopolitical risks, and European energy taxes; and business strategy, projects, production, earnings factors, volumes, sales, and performance across Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, Specialty Products, and Corporate and Financing. It also reviews segment developments and financial results, capital investment and allocation, cash flows, liquidity, debt, shareholder distributions, contractual obligations, guarantees, and legal uncertainties.

nodes.title: CAPITAL AND EXPLORATION EXPENDITURES
nodes.summary: Defines Capex as before-tax property, plant and equipment additions plus exploration expenses, including equity-company shares, with specified asset-acquisition and exploration-equipment exclusions; management focuses on controllable spending. A regional and business-segment table compares 2022 and 2021 Capex. Spending was $22.7 billion in 2022; planned 2023 investment is $23–25 billion, including $11.6 billion in firm commitments, with another $11.4 billion committed for 2024 onward, subject to project progress and acquisitions. Upstream spending rose 39% to $17.0 billion, driven by the Permian and Guyana. Projects can take years to produce; developed reserves were 63% of proved reserves, above 60% for a decade. Energy Products spending rose $0.4 billion to $2.4 billion, Chemical Products rose $0.9 billion to $3.0 billion, and Specialty Products fell $0.1 billion to $0.3 billion.

nodes.title: TAXES
nodes.summary: In 2022, ExxonMobil recorded $51.6 billion in total taxes, including $20.2 billion in income tax expense at a 33% effective rate, and $31.5 billion in other taxes and duties. In 2021, total taxes were $40.6 billion; income tax expense was $7.6 billion, the effective rate was 31%, and other taxes and duties were $33.0 billion. Environmental expenditures were $5.7 billion in 2022 ($3.8 billion in expenses and $1.9 billion in capital spending), versus $4.6 billion in 2021. The company expects spending to rise to $7.3 billion in 2023 and $8.2 billion in 2024, with capital shares of 46% and 51%. It describes pollution-prevention and remediation efforts, accounting for probable, estimable environmental obligations, and potential shared liability at multi-party sites; no individual site is expected to cause material losses. Environmental provisions were $185 million in 2022, and liabilities were $730 million at year-end, versus $146 million and $807 million in 2021.

nodes.title: MARKET RISKS
nodes.summary: The text reports 2020–2022 worldwide average oil/NGL and natural-gas realizations and explains how commodity-price movements affect Upstream earnings, while noting that actual impacts depend on product mix, trading, taxes, contract lags, and volumes. Refining and chemical earnings depend chiefly on margins and market conditions; prolonged adverse markets make financial strength important. It describes integrated, market-priced intersegment trade, long-term supply-and-demand economics, investment evaluation including greenhouse-gas costs, and disciplined asset divestments. Risk management covers diversification, derivatives and controls, counterparty protections, immaterial interest-rate and currency exposures, liquidity and debt funding, and potential joint-venture funding constraints.

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES
key_items: Outlook for Energy and Cash Flow Assessment; Fair Value of Impaired Assets
Outlook for Energy and Cash Flow Assessment
Asset Retirement Obligations; Suspended Exploratory Well Costs
Pension Benefits; Litigation and Tax Contingencies
nodes.summary: The text outlines critical accounting estimates and judgments: reserve estimation, classification, revisions, and their use in unit-of-production depreciation; impairment monitoring, cash-flow assumptions, fair-value methods, other asset-specific tests, historical impairment charges, and future risk factors; asset retirement obligations and suspended exploratory well costs; pension plans, funding, assumptions, returns, and expense sensitivity; and accounting, disclosure, and judgment for litigation and uncertain tax contingencies. It also describes how the Corporate Plan and energy outlook inform impairment assessments, including emissions costs and climate goals.

nodes.title: MANAGEMENT’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL REPORTING
key_items: Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting; Basis for Opinions; Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Opinions on the Financial Statements and Internal Control over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
The Impact of Proved Oil and Natural Gas Reserves on Upstream Property, Plant and Equipment, Net
nodes.summary: Management states it is responsible for financial-reporting controls, evaluated them under COSO’s 2013 framework, and found them effective as of December 31, 2022; executives are identified as signatories. PwC’s report gives unqualified opinions that Exxon Mobil’s 2020–2022 consolidated financial statements fairly present its financial position and results under U.S. GAAP and that controls were effective. It describes management and auditor responsibilities, audit procedures, reasonable assurance, and inherent control limitations. The critical audit matter is proved oil and gas reserve estimates’ effect on upstream PP&E and depreciation; PwC tested controls, specialists’ qualifications, methods, assumptions and data, including future development costs. PwC signed in Dallas on February 22, 2023, and reports serving as auditor since 1934.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF INCOME
nodes.summary: Consolidated income statement for 2022, 2021, and 2020, in millions of dollars, showing sales and other operating revenue, equity-affiliate income and other income; total revenues; operating and other costs, including purchases, production, administration, depreciation, exploration, pension, interest, and taxes; income before taxes, income tax expense or benefit, net income including noncontrolling interests, income attributable to noncontrolling interests and to ExxonMobil, and basic and diluted earnings per common share. Notes are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
key_items: Net income (loss) including noncontrolling interests Other comprehensive income (loss) (net of income taxes)
nodes.summary: A consolidated statement of comprehensive income presents 2022, 2021, and 2020 figures in millions of dollars. It reports net income or loss including noncontrolling interests; other comprehensive income or loss, net of taxes, with foreign-exchange translation adjustments and postretirement-benefit reserve adjustments and related amortization or settlement; total other comprehensive income or loss; comprehensive income or loss including noncontrolling interests; and amounts attributable to noncontrolling interests and ExxonMobil. The accompanying financial-statement notes are integral to the statement.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED BALANCE SHEET
key_items: Current assets; Total current assets; Total Assets; Current liabilities; ExxonMobil share of equity
nodes.summary: Consolidated balance sheets for December 31, 2022 and 2021, in millions of dollars, present assets (current assets, investments and long-term receivables, property and equipment, and other assets), liabilities (current and long-term), commitments and contingencies, and equity. Equity includes common stock, reinvested earnings, accumulated other comprehensive income, treasury stock, ExxonMobil’s equity share, and noncontrolling interests. Notes to the financial statements are integral to the statements.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF CASH FLOWS
nodes.summary: Consolidated statements of cash flows for 2022, 2021, and 2020, in millions of dollars, report operating activities (net income and noncash adjustments, working-capital changes, and other items), investing activities (property additions, asset-sale proceeds, investments, and other flows), and financing activities (debt, commercial paper, dividends, noncontrolling interests, and share repurchases). They also show exchange-rate effects and beginning, change in, and ending cash balances. A footnote clarifies the short-term debt classification; financial statement notes are integral.

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENT OF CHANGES IN EQUITY
nodes.summary: The consolidated statement of changes in equity reports ExxonMobil’s 2019–2022 balances and annual movements, including stock-based award amortization, other items, net income or loss, common dividends, accounting changes, other comprehensive income, acquisitions, and dispositions. It also presents common-share activity, issued and treasury shares, and noncontrolling interests. The notes state that management is responsible for the statements, outline the company’s energy and lower-emission businesses, explain that GAAP estimates affect reported amounts and actual results may differ, and note that prior-year figures were sometimes reclassified for 2022 presentation.

Presents ExxonMobil’s 2020–2022 financial results, cash flow, capital employed, returns, structural cost savings, segment earnings reconciliations, and definitions of non-GAAP measures. Covers forward-looking-statement risks, business strategy and environment, capital and exploration spending, taxes and environmental obligations, market risks, and critical accounting estimates. Also includes management’s internal-control assessment, the auditor’s opinions and critical audit matter, and consolidated income, comprehensive income, balance sheet, cash flow, and changes-in-equity statements.

Covers ExxonMobil stock, dividends, repurchases, and market-risk disclosures; financial statements, auditor reports, controls, and related disclosures; proxy-related governance and compensation matters and equity-plan data; and Part IV’s financial statements and exhibits. It also presents business-profile comparisons by segment and geography, financial results and cash flows, capital and returns, segment reconciliations, strategy and risk discussions, taxes, environmental obligations, critical accounting estimates, internal-control assessments, and supplemental oil and gas information.

summary: Reports gross and net undeveloped acreage by region and ownership type for 2022 and 2021, with explanatory notes and rights, work-program, relinquishment, extension, and expiration practices. Describes hydrocarbon licensing and contract terms across the United States, Canada, the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Oceania. Also covers ExxonMobil’s refining network and capacity, retail fuel sites and announced asset sales, petrochemical complex capacities and calculation conventions, specified environmental legal proceedings, nonapplicable mine-safety disclosures and executive-officer information, and the broader Part II financial, market, governance, risk, control, and oil-and-gas disclosures.

title: 1. Summary of Accounting Policies

nodes.title: Consolidation, Investments, and Revenue Recognition
key_items: Principles of Consolidation and Accounting for Investments
nodes.summary: Consolidation covers controlled subsidiaries, qualifying variable-interest entities, and upstream interests; significant-influence investments use the equity method, with impairment testing, foreign-currency translation adjustments, and fair-value or modified-cost measurement for other equity securities. Revenue is recognized when customers take control, generally at market-based prices; estimated indexed prices are later finalized. The policy also addresses payment terms, future deliveries, inventory exchanges, ASC 606 and non-ASC 606 receivables, and immaterial contract assets and liabilities.

nodes.title: Tax, Derivative, Fair Value, and Inventory Policies
nodes.summary: The Corporation excludes certain sales and value-added taxes collected for governments from revenue, reports other such taxes gross, and records U.S. tax on global intangible low-taxed income as incurred. Derivatives may manage exposures or be used for trading; they are generally measured at fair value, with eligible netting, and gains and losses are recognized according to whether hedge accounting is applied and whether the hedge is fair value or cash flow. Fair value inputs are classified into three levels by observability. Crude oil, product, and merchandise inventories use the lower of market value or cost, generally LIFO; inventory costs include directly and indirectly incurred costs, while selling and administrative expenses are excluded. Materials and supplies are carried at cost or less.

nodes.title: Property, Plant, and Equipment
nodes.summary: The text explains the Corporation’s successful-efforts accounting for exploration and production costs, capitalization and expensing rules, and depreciation, depletion, amortization, maintenance, and asset retirements. It describes impairment indicators, monitoring, long-term price and margin assumptions, and why standardized reserve cash-flow measures are not used for impairment decisions. Recoverability forecasts draw on the Board-approved Corporate Plan and Outlook for Energy, including production, prices, costs, emissions plans and carbon costs. Impaired assets are measured at fair value; unproved properties and assets held for sale receive separate impairment assessments, and property-sale gains are recognized subject to specified conditions.

nodes.title: Environmental Liabilities and Currency Translation
nodes.summary: Environmental liabilities are recognized when obligations are probable and estimable, without reducing them for third-party recoveries or discounting expected cash expenditures. Functional currencies for international subsidiaries reflect their economic environments: Product Solutions generally uses local currencies, with U.S. dollars in high-inflation countries and Singapore; self-contained Canadian and European Upstream operations use local currencies, while certain Asian and African operations use U.S. dollars. Foreign-currency transaction remeasurement gains and losses are included in income.

summary: The section outlines policies for consolidation, investments and equity securities; revenue recognition and related contracts and receivables; taxes; derivative use, fair-value measurement and hedge accounting; and inventory valuation. It explains successful-efforts accounting for exploration and production, capitalization, depreciation and impairment of property and equipment, including forecasts and asset sales. It also covers recognition of environmental liabilities and functional-currency choices and foreign-currency remeasurement for international operations.

title: 2. Russia
summary: In response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the Corporation planned to exit the Sakhalin-1 project and determined its assets were unrecoverable, recording first-quarter after-tax impairment charges of $3.4 billion ($4.6 billion before tax), mostly in depreciation and depletion. Russia terminated its interests on October 14 and transferred operations to a Russian operator; the fourth quarter included a $1.1 billion after-tax benefit related largely to changes in Sakhalin obligations. The exit removed about 150 million oil-equivalent barrels from year-end proved reserves.

title: 3. Miscellaneous Financial Information
summary: The notes report R&D expenses and foreign-exchange losses for 2020–2022; LIFO-related income gains and the excess replacement cost of inventory over LIFO carrying value; and year-end 2021–2022 inventory by crude oil, petroleum products, chemical products, and gas/other, with chemical products defined. They describe a 2020 goodwill impairment, its causes, valuation basis, and income-statement classification; workforce-reduction charges, completion, reserves, and cash payments; and government assistance, including energy-price reimbursements, receivables, program variability and expected impact, plus cap-and-trade allowances and their accounting.

Income Tax (Expense)/Credit For Components of Other Comprehensive Income

They also disclose net investment hedge gains, before-tax amounts reclassified to income for foreign-exchange translation and postretirement-benefit costs, and income tax expenses or credits for these components.

summary: Explains cash-equivalent classification and details asset-sale gains or losses and impairment effects in cash-flow statements for 2020–2022, alongside income taxes and cash interest paid. Presents 2022 and 2021 balances for receivables, notes and loans payable, and accounts payable and accrued liabilities. Describes receivable accounting and customer credit comparability, unused short-term credit lines, and borrowing interest rates.
